title: Ordered selections
parts: The number of ways to select and order r objects from n distinct objects.
example: From 5 people, there are 5×4=20 ways to choose a chair and a different secretary.
note: Swapping the chair and secretary gives a different outcome.
wrong: The number of selections when order is ignored.

title: Unordered selections
parts: The number of ways to choose r objects from n distinct objects without regard to order.
example: There are 6 pairs of people in a group of 4, so 4C2=6.
note: Choosing A then B gives the same pair as choosing B then A.
wrong: The number of arrangements when order matters.

title: Probability of an event
parts: The chance that event A occurs.
example: On a fair die, if A is rolling a 6, P(A)=1/6.
note: A probability lies between 0 and 1 inclusive.
wrong: The number of outcomes in A, irrespective of how likely they are.

title: Sample space
parts: The possible outcomes of this trial are heads and tails.
example: A single coin toss has these two outcomes.
note: The sample space contains all possible outcomes. An event can contain only some of them.
wrong: The event that a single toss is both heads and tails.

title: Complement of an event
parts: The probability that A does not happen.
note: The complement includes every outcome outside A in the sample space.
wrong: The probability that A happens twice.

title: Addition rule for probabilities
notation: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
parts: The chance at least one event occurs
is the sum of their chances with the overlap subtracted once.
example: If P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4 and P(A∩B)=0.2, the union has probability 0.7.
note: Adding the two probabilities alone double counts the overlap.
wrong: The chance that both events occur.

title: First success on a specified trial
parts: The first n−1 independent trials fail
example: A first head on toss 3 has probability ½×½×½=⅛.
note: This specifies exactly where the first success occurs.
wrong: The probability of one success anywhere in n trials.

title: Sample size
parts: Thirty observations are in the sample.
example: If a school with 600 pupils surveys 30 of them, its sample size is n=30.
note: A sample size is a count, and is distinct from the population size.

title: Equal chance in a simple random sample
parts: In a simple random sample of size n from N people, each person has this chance of inclusion.
example: Randomly choosing 10 distinct names from 100 gives each person inclusion probability 0.1.
note: Equal inclusion chances do not guarantee any particular mix of people in one sample.
wrong: The entire set of n names has probability n/N of being selected.

title: Interquartile range
parts: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile.
example: If Q₁=6 and Q₃=14, the IQR is 8.
note: IQR measures the spread of the middle half. The full range uses the minimum and maximum.
wrong: Subtract the smallest observation from the largest.

title: Relative frequency
parts: The number in a category divided by the total number of observations.
example: If 12 of 40 responses are Yes, the relative frequency is 0.3.
note: Frequency is a count. Relative frequency is a fraction or percentage.
wrong: Divide the total sample size by the count in the category.

title: Margin of error for a proportion
parts: The approximate maximum 95% margin of error for a sample proportion from a simple random sample.
example: For n=400 the margin is about 1/20=0.05, or five percentage points.
note: It estimates sampling uncertainty. It cannot correct a biased sample.
wrong: The proportion of all responses that were wrong.
